title: Decide whether adversarial review should be automatic
description:
## Question

**Surfaced by the correction-patterns research — the pattern nobody named, and second-largest by raw count.**

66 instances across ~20 projects (55 in Claude Code, 11 in Codex) of Frank routing already-finished work to a second adversarial reviewer rather than accepting the completion report:

> "Yes please do. Then let a subagent review it again and be very critical" — `history.jsonl:1803`

> "Look at the changes this feature branch introduces. Look at them with a critical and skeptical mind. Assume mistakes were made, anti-patterns…" — Codex rollout 2026-06-04, repeated verbatim on 06-05

> "Let a subagent review the unit tests, let it be critical. Watch out for improper mocks. Are we testing the real implementation?" — `history.jsonl:2048`

> "Could you use codex-reviewer to verify these findings?" — `history.jsonl:5265`

And the meta-version, asking why a completed report was wrong at all:

> "Why did the explore subagent come up with the wrong information? Could you analyse that?" — `history.jsonl:5956`

This costs a full extra review cycle on essentially every non-trivial task, and it is currently manual every single time.

Decide:
- Is this a *symptom* of the runtime-verification gap (fix that and the ritual stops being needed), or an independent standing preference (Frank wants adversarial review regardless)? The research argues they are one failure seen from two sides — but that is `[inferred]`, not measured.
- If it stays: should `reviewer` and/or `codex-review` fire automatically rather than on request, and at which task tier? Note `orchestrator.md:189-190` currently makes post-task review *optional* and gates `codex-review` to Standard/Complex.
- What does the reviewer need in order to be worth its cost? `reviewer.md:20-28` has no item for any of the six measured correction patterns.

Interacts directly with *Close the reported-done-but-does-not-run gap* and with the model-routing ticket (`reviewer` currently runs on sonnet with a 20-turn cap).

Evidence: `docs/agents/correction-patterns-2026-08-10.md`, pattern 2.

title: Close the reported-done-but-does-not-run gap
description:
## Question

"Verify in the browser or through other means" is a recurring manual ask, and the parts already exist and are unwired: the `browser` agent (`agent-browser` CLI, sonnet, 20 turns) is invoked by nothing automatically, and `build-runner` is invoked ad hoc.

Design the loop that makes verification the default tail of a change rather than a thing to remember. Decide the trigger (which changes warrant runtime verification), what "verified" means for a UI change vs. a service change, and whether this chains off the producing skill or stands alone.

The verification-loops post's chained pattern is the reference shape.
notes:
BLOCKED BY: Bring the 11 unversioned agents under version control (dotfiles_nvim-tabs-sidebar-vtq.2)
EVIDENCE (from the correction-patterns research): this is the #1 pattern by a wide margin - 81 runtime-failure reports across 15 repos, 28 of them explicitly 'still' broken AFTER a fix was applied, 41 requests to drive a browser. Not an Angular quirk: spans code/hfs, .config/nvim, code/loom, code/claude-skills-marketplace, Sync.

Root cause named in the research: the agent reports completion on the strength of having WRITTEN the code, not on the strength of having OBSERVED it work.

Verbatim: 'You havent tested it turly. Because pnpm storybook ends up with a broken build' (history.jsonl:3999); 'First run the tests and verify THEN fix the code' (:4469); 'Dockers are up, but still nothing I think.' (:7529).

Design this as the default tail of a change, not a thing to remember. Note the sibling ticket on automatic adversarial review - the research argues they are one failure seen from two sides, so decide deliberately whether they are one loop or two.

title: Restore the gutted settings.json and rewire the enforcement guard
description:
## Question

`claude/.claude/settings.json` has an uncommitted `-66/+17` diff that removed the enforcement hooks. Current wiring is only `claude-capture`, `rtk hook claude`, `hooked budget`, and `bd prime`. `settings.json.bak` references `claude-hook-guard` twice and `enforce-orchestrator` once; the current file references neither, nor `enforce-explore-delegation.sh` or `scope-search.sh`.

Restore the guard, then **prove it enforces** — not by reading config, but by attempting a denied command from the main agent and from a subagent and observing the denial. Then commit.

Open sub-questions:
- Was the deletion deliberate (something broke) or accidental? Check reflog and session history before restoring.
- `scope-search.sh` and `enforce-explore-delegation.sh` appear never to have been wired at all, even in the `.bak`. Were they ever active?
- `enforce-explore-delegation.sh` duplicates a restriction `rules.toml` already expresses — `profiles.orchestrator` and `profiles.main` grant no `Glob`/`Grep`. Wire one, not both.

**Why this blocks the map:** the answer decides whether agent prose about "the rule engine" is redundant (delete it) or load-bearing (keep it). Every prose-deletion ticket depends on it.

Settled during charting: option (a) — restore-then-simplify.
notes:
STRICTNESS SIMULATION (replayed rules.toml tool-allowlists against 113,895 PreToolUse events in hooked's sessions.db).

Tool-level denial rate: 23,464 / 113,895 = 20%. This is a FLOOR - the simulation models only the per-profile 'tools' allowlist, not the Bash command-category allowlists or the agent.spawn.allow list, both of which deny further.

The 20% is NOT distributed the way you would fear. Your own agents' profiles fit almost perfectly:
  worker 26,881 calls / 0% denied
  search 23,917 / 0%
  git 6,256 / 0%
  build-runner 6,064 / 0%
  codex-review 1,719 / 0%   notes 1,523 / 0%   browser 1,390 / 0%
  curl 976 / 0%   docker 735 / 0%   ast-search 11 / 0%
  reviewer 3,746 / 3% (Bash only)   docs 436 / 0%

Nearly all denial comes from agent types with NO PROFILE, which fall through to profiles._default = {Skill}:
  Explore            14,808 calls / 99% denied  <- BUILT-IN Claude Code agent
  general-purpose     2,281 / 99%               <- BUILT-IN
  workflow-subagent     529 / 100%              <- BUILT-IN
  claude-code-guide     172 / 100%              <- BUILT-IN
  plus ~15 ad-hoc named subagents (git-recon, rule-mover, code-verify, jira-*, search-recon, git-merge, ...) all at 100%
That is ~18,000 of the 23,464 denials - fail-closed defaults meeting an open world of agent types.

Second cluster - the main agent, 5,918 calls / 49% denied: Bash 1,493, Edit 547, ToolSearch 234, Write 187. profiles.main grants no Bash and no Edit at all.

Third - RULESET DRIFT. ToolSearch and SendMessage show up as denials across orchestrator (400 + 185) and Plan. These are current Claude Code machinery the ruleset predates. Same for several MCP tools.

CONCLUSION for this ticket: do not re-enable claude-hook-guard unchanged. Two structural gaps to fix first: (1) profiles._default is fail-closed with no coverage for built-in or ad-hoc agent types; (2) claude-hook-guard has NO warn-only/dry-run/observe mode - grep across its src, toml and md returns zero matches for dry-run|observe|warn-only|audit|shadow|permissive. It is binary deny.

By contrast 'hooked' already implements graduated enforcement: 'hooked gate' is an explicitly non-blocking PreToolUse coverage gate (warns once per file), and 'hooked budget' classifies Ok -> Warn60 -> Warn85 -> Deny. That is the shape a rollout should have.
IMPLEMENTED (warn-only, not yet wired):
- 4 built-in profiles added (explore, general-purpose, workflow-subagent, claude-code-guide) - verified to resolve and allow Read. 21 profiles total, up from 17.
- ToolSearch/SendMessage/WebSearch/SendUserFile/TaskStop/Monitor + plan-mode tools added to orchestrator/main/plan; orchestrator+main Bash widened to bd-read, bd-write, git-read, ls, fs-read-introspection, jq, cass. Glob/Grep and fs-search deliberately withheld as the delegation steer.
- KNOWN_NATIVE_TOOLS in src/config.rs extended by 8 entries - without this, load_config rejected the file and main.rs:126-131 FAILS CLOSED, denying every tool call from every agent.
- NEW: warn-only mode. --warn-only flag or CLAUDE_HOOK_GUARD_WARN_ONLY=1|true. Emits no deny, prints WOULD-DENY to stderr, appends JSONL to ~/.claude/telemetry/guard-denials.jsonl (override via CLAUDE_HOOK_GUARD_LOG). Write failures swallowed - telemetry never blocks a call. New src/audit.rs + Engine::resolve_profile_id. No new crate deps.

FOUR POLICY-TEST FAILURES NOW EXPOSED. tests/config_policy_tests.rs is a policy SPECIFICATION and three of these are caused by the widening above, NOT pre-existing bugs (a subagent misattributed them; verified by reading the assertions):
1. orchestrator_bash_is_limited_to_bd_cli - asserts 'git status' is denied for orchestrator. Adding git-read broke it. The codified intent was 'orchestrator Bash = bd only'. DECIDE: update the test to the new intent, or narrow the profile back.
2. bd_write_commands_are_limited_to_orchestrator_and_worker - asserts profile 'main' cannot mutate beads. Adding bd-write to profiles.main broke it. Note profiles.main is near-dead code anyway (see below) - reverting its widening may be the better fix.
3. global_bd_access_rejects_shell_composition - expects denial text 'Tool Bash not allowed' for main running 'bd list && bd status'. Still DENIED (structure rule), but the message changed because main now has Bash. Assertion needs updating; behaviour is fine.
4. github_cli_is_not_global_bash_access - asserts worker cannot run 'gh pr view'. Caused by Frank's own uncommitted gh-pr category (commented 'II-7992 ... Added on request'), NOT by this work.

TWO STRUCTURAL FINDINGS:
- profiles.main is effectively dead code. profiles.orchestrator has aliases = ["", "orchestrator"], so a null agent_type (the real main agent) resolves to ORCHESTRATOR. profiles.main only fires on a literal 'main'. Consider deleting it rather than maintaining two seats.
- engine.rs:92's bespoke message 'BLOCKED: Delegate Glob/Grep to the search profile' is gated on profile_id == "main" and therefore NEVER fires for the real main agent - verified: the actual denial is the generic 'Tool Glob not allowed for profile orchestrator'. Either change the gate to orchestrator or drop the special case.

STILL RED, unrelated: tests/agent_registry_tests.rs::agent_registry_is_consistent - stale Explore reference + CLAUDE.md missing agents/browser.md. Pre-existing (fails identically before and after). Note this test cross-checks CLAUDE.md against agent files - an existing verification loop, currently red.
WIRED IN WARN-ONLY 2026-08-10. settings.json now has 3 PreToolUse entries (claude-capture, rtk hook claude, claude-hook-guard) plus CLAUDE_HOOK_GUARD_WARN_ONLY=1 in env. Both pre-existing entries intact; no other hook event count changed. The 7 previously-removed hook entries were NOT restored - that remains this ticket's open decision.

FIRST DATA, and it contradicts the simulation. Within minutes the log had 11 entries and EVERY ONE was:
  reason: 'BLOCKED: profile only allows a single command.'  profile: orchestrator  tool: Bash
That is the structure rule (single-command = true, no-redirection = true), NOT a tool-allowlist or command-category denial. The strictness simulation modelled tools and categories and therefore could not see this at all.

Real examples logged: multi-line Bash with 'cd X\nls Y\necho Z', and compound one-liners joined with ';'. Entries arrived from a concurrent session doing ast-grep i18n work in code/hfs/feature-II-8571 as well as from this one, so this is ordinary working behaviour, not an artefact of the analysis session.

IMPLICATION: the dominant real-world cost of this ruleset is not 'which tools' or 'which commands' - it is 'no compound shell lines'. That is a much more invasive constraint than the profile design suggests, and it applies to the orchestrator seat where most interactive work happens. Whether single-command/no-redirection should stay is now a live question and probably belongs with the delegation decision.

This is exactly what warn-only was for: it surfaced in minutes a constraint that a static analysis of 113,895 events could not.

SETTINGS.JSON REGRESSION - READ THE DIFF, IT IS NOT AN ACCIDENT. The uncommitted -66/+17 mixes wanted config (model opus[1m], effortLevel high->xhigh, tui fullscreen, agent-teams + LSP env vars, 4 new plugins incl mattpocock-skills, marketplace local path, aws permissions) with removal of SEVEN hook entries: claude-hook-guard on all-tools AND on Glob|Grep, enforce-orchestrator.sh, hooked gate, hooked budget on PreToolUse, hooked budget on PostToolUse, coverage-autowrite.sh. The guard entry was REPLACED IN PLACE by 'rtk hook claude' rather than deleted, which reads as a deliberate swap of the hook stack for RTK, not a botched edit. So the remaining decision is 'do we want the WS1/WS2 provenance+budget stack back', not 'repair a mistake'.

GOTCHA: RTK filters git output through the Bash hook - 'git diff' returns a stat with no body. Redirect to a file first: git --no-pager diff --no-color -- <path> > /tmp/x.diff

title: Bring the 11 unversioned agents under version control
description:
## Question

Only `orchestrator.md`, `search.md`, and `worker.md` are symlinked into `~/.dotfiles/claude/.claude/agents/`. These 11 exist solely as loose files in `~/.claude/agents/` with no version control:

`ast-search.md`, `browser.md`, `build-runner.md`, `codex-review.md`, `curl.md`, `docker.md`, `docs.md`, `git.md`, `lsp-search.md`, `notes.md`, `reviewer.md`

Move them into the stow package, symlink them back, and commit — so every later rewrite is revertible.

Also decide whether the unwired hook scripts (`enforce-orchestrator.sh`, `enforce-explore-delegation.sh`, `scope-search.sh`, `capture.sh`, `session-start.sh`, `session-end.sh`) and `~/.claude/tools/claude-hook-guard/` belong in the same package.

**Why this blocks the map:** every agent-rewrite ticket edits these files. Doing that without a revert path is not acceptable.

title: Repair bd's broken dependency graph
description:
## Question

`bd dep list <id>` and `bd stats` both fail with `Error 1105: column "depends_on_id" could not be found in any table in scope` on bd 1.0.4 in embedded-dolt mode. `bd ready` runs but its blocker-awareness cannot be trusted while the dependency reads fail.

What is the fix — a Dolt schema migration, a `bd init --force` reimport from `.beads/issues.jsonl`, a switch to server mode, or an upstream bug to report?

`bd doctor` is unsupported in embedded mode. Preserve the 5 pre-existing issues and this map's children.

**Why this blocks the map:** Wayfinder needs native blocking edges to render the frontier. Until dep writes and reads both work, this map's blocking relationships cannot be wired and `bd ready` cannot be used to pick the next ticket.
notes: SEVERITY ESCALATED. The bug is not limited to dependency queries - 'bd close' itself fails ('Error checking blockers ... depends_on_id'), so the tracker cannot close issues at all. Workaround in use for this map: 'bd update <id> --status closed'. Also confirmed broken: all 'bd dep --blocks' writes, every parent-child dependency row at creation time, 'bd dep list', 'bd stats'. The issue tree still RENDERS correctly, which makes this silently wrong rather than loudly broken.

title: Design the i18n key verification loop
description: ## Question **Surfaced by the correction-patterns research — the most consistent code-level correction, and on nobody's list.** 15 correction prompts across 6 distinct HFS worktrees, 2025-11-07 → 2026-08-02. Three sub-modes: **Missing entirely** > "There's a missing translation. The noABN. It's missing in the portals I believe" — `history.jsonl:6399` > "The baseline translation.json wasnt updated, could you do that?" — `:6810` > "I see that there's no translations in the action list … `offer.actions.profile`" — `:7499` **New key invented instead of reusing the canonical one** > "I see registrationv2.zipCodeLabel. Why not use the default zip code (or postal code) translation from common.form.address?" — `:7837` > "Try to use the translation keys already present. Most of them are in common.form" — `:3645` **Wired but broken at runtime** > "the translation key is: common.form.phoneNumber.error.combinationInvalid — But the translations are not nested in that way. In the JSONs its common.form.error.phoneNumber" — `:4205` This is the textbook case from the verification-loops post: a deterministic, repo-specific rule no generic linter catches. All three sub-modes are checkable against a diff plus the translation JSONs — does every new key exist, does an equivalent key already exist elsewhere, does the nesting match. Scope caveat to weigh: confined to the HFS monorepo. That makes it a project-level skill rather than a global one — but it recurs across six independent worktrees over nine months, so it is systemic rather than one bad ticket. Decide where it lives. Evidence: `docs/agents/correction-patterns-2026-08-10.md`, pattern 4.

title: Rewrite CLAUDE.md under evidence-over-guidance
description:
## Question

Apply the rule to both files — `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (51 lines, global) and `~/CLAUDE.md` (103 lines, project): every surviving rule must name a concrete failure it prevents. Rules that cannot name one get deleted; rules that can, keep a one-line justification.

Known duplication to resolve, not preserve:
- Verification discipline stated four times — `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md:38-44`, `orchestrator.md:173-178`, `worker.md:99`, `search.md:75-76`
- Task sizing stated twice, near-verbatim — `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md:26-34`, `orchestrator.md:64-72`
- Nine agent files defer to a rule engine — whether that prose survives depends on the guard-rewiring ticket

The context-engineering post's target shape for CLAUDE.md is a brief repo description plus gotchas discoverable only from the codebase, with everything else behind progressive disclosure. Treat that as the direction, not the mandate — divergences get written down.

Depends on the guard rewiring and the delegation decision: what is redundant cannot be known until both land.

title: Design the model and effort routing policy
description:
## Question

Every agent pins a model statically and none set an effort level: `search`/`docs`/`git`/`notes`/`codex-review`/`ast-search`/`lsp-search`/`curl`/`docker` on haiku, `worker`/`reviewer`/`build-runner`/`browser` on sonnet, `orchestrator` unset. These pins predate effort levels entirely.

Produce the routing policy: model and effort per agent, plus whether to adopt the advisor pattern (cheap worker calls a smarter model to check its plan and evaluate its work — reported at within 10% of top-tier quality at 63% of the price).

Constraints settled during charting: all models and effort levels are available, but Fable has limited capacity, so **Opus 5 is the default top tier and advisor tier**.

Specific things to challenge: `reviewer` is the adversarial quality gate and runs on sonnet with a 20-turn cap — the post says spend up where judgment matters most. And "cost-per-task is often lower for more intelligent models at lower effort" directly inverts the assumption behind pinning `search` to haiku.

title: Diagnose why skill-driven output still lands wrong
description:
## Question

`worker.md:22-46` already mandates skill invocation before coding and routes 8 Angular file types to `striive-frontend:*` skills — which do exist at `~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/claude-skills-marketplace/plugins/striive-frontend`. Wrong patterns still land.

So the failure is not "the agent skipped the skill." Determine which it is:
- the skill's own guidance is wrong or stale
- the agent invokes it and then diverges
- the routing picks the wrong skill
- the skill is right but silent on the case that goes wrong

The fix differs completely per cause: fix the skill, add a verification loop, fix the routing, or extend the skill. Do not guess — get examples.
notes:
BLOCKED BY: Mine session history for recurring correction patterns (dotfiles_nvim-tabs-sidebar-vtq.5)
UNBLOCKED - its blocker (Mine session history for recurring correction patterns) is closed.

The research confirms the pattern (14 instances, 4 repos) and - importantly - splits it into two modes that need different fixes:

(a) The skill encodes a wrong or missing rule:
  'The angular-component skill should have mentioned that we dont want custom css but prefer primeflex classes' (history.jsonl:5913)
  'I actually don't want to use effect() and untracked with forms, does the skill mention it should be built that way' (:4434)
  'the team-pr-dashboard skill doesn't filter the PRs upfront but just retrieves ALL open PRs' (:3813)

(b) The skill was right and the agent diverged - the sharper half:
  'I saw that recruiter-edit.form.ts doesn't use the form-type-helper.ts. I thought the /angular-form skill mentioned to use those.' (:7114)
  'Which instructions were NOT followed?' (:7117, :7118 - asked twice)
  'Any reason why the subagents didn't use the proper skill when working on the angularjs migration?' (Codex rollout 2026-04-02)

Scope correction: this is NOT a general-purpose-skill problem. It is concentrated in the HFS Angular-migration skill family (angular-component, angular-form, angularjs-migrate-context, angularjs-migrate-plan) plus team-pr-dashboard and loom.

Frank has already institutionalised a fix attempt: 'Could you create an epic bead per angular skill and research if the skill has any contradictions, use of anti-patterns, lacking reference material, lack of clear instructions?' (:7176). Check whether those beads exist before starting.

Evidence: docs/agents/correction-patterns-2026-08-10.md, pattern 3.

title: Design the reuse-before-writing loop
description:
## Question

**This ticket replaces "Design the SOLID-adherence review loop", whose premise the research refuted.**

Searching 8,007 prompts for SOLID and every related principle returned 4 hits, and every one is Frank asking for a review *against* SOLID up front. There are **zero** instances of him naming a SOLID principle to correct code an agent had just finished.

What he actually types, 16 times across 9 projects, is a concrete reuse pointer:

> "You should not modify the addressInputComponent but use the new address selectors. I believe its already used for super-striive" — `history.jsonl:1953`

> "I see that we have AfasCountries which fill in a p-dropdown with the countries. However, we should just use app-country-select and we shouldn't fetch AfasCountries since that should be deprecated" — `history.jsonl:3658`

> "This code … Should not become methods inside the component. These should be made into pure pipes to reuse elsewhere" — `history.jsonl:3654`

> "We already have Tree-sitter parsing, so I would love to use that instead of custom regex." — `history.jsonl:378`

So the loop to build is not a principle checker. It is: **before writing a new implementation, find out whether a shared one already exists** — and after writing, flag anything that duplicates something reachable in the repo.

Decide: does this run *before* the work (a discovery step in the producing skill) or *after* it (a diff-time duplication check)? Before is more valuable and much harder — the agent has to know what to search for. Consider whether the existing `search` / `lsp-search` agents already give enough surface, or whether this needs a repo-specific index of shared components.

Evidence: `docs/agents/correction-patterns-2026-08-10.md`, pattern 5.
notes: BLOCKED BY: Bring the 11 unversioned agents under version control (dotfiles_nvim-tabs-sidebar-vtq.2); Mine session history for recurring correction patterns (dotfiles_nvim-tabs-sidebar-vtq.5)

title: Decide how much delegation-first survives Claude 5
description:
## Question

`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md:3-17` makes delegation mandatory across ~10 categories. `orchestrator.md:33-37` forbids the orchestrator from editing files, running shell commands, or using Glob/Grep/LSP/AST directly. That architecture was designed when context was scarce and model judgment weaker; Claude 5 has 1M context and the sources argue directly against blanket constraints.

Decide the policy: fully mandatory, delegate-by-default with judgment for narrow lookups, or advisory only. Then decide what the restored hook guard should enforce — the two questions have the same answer.

Concrete cost to weigh: a two-file lookup currently costs a subagent spawn, a report round-trip, and an orchestrator verification pass, to save context there is now a million tokens of. Against that, delegation still buys parallel fan-out, cheap-model cost savings, and context isolation on large sweeps.

Deferred from charting by explicit request — this gets its own session.

title: Mine session history for recurring correction patterns
description:
## Question

Three recurring manual corrections were named from memory during charting: comments that should be removed, SOLID violations, and missing runtime/browser verification. A fourth — "mistakes introduced through skills" — is real but unlocalised.

Mine the actual record for what gets corrected, how often, and in which repos:
- `~/.claude/history.jsonl` (~2.2MB)
- `cass search --mode lexical` across Codex and Claude Code sessions

Note: `cass` semantic assets are missing (`consent required for model download`) and the index was 51 minutes stale at charting; lexical mode works, or run `cass index --full` first.

Return a ranked list of correction patterns with frequency and example citations. This is evidence for the three loop-design tickets and for the skills diagnosis — it may also surface a pattern nobody remembered.
notes:
RESOLVED. Full findings: docs/agents/correction-patterns-2026-08-10.md (in this repo).

Corpus: 8,007 typed prompts in ~/.claude/history.jsonl (complete, 2025-10-14 -> 2026-08-09), 350 surviving session transcripts, 616 Codex rollouts. Counts are manually validated, not raw regex hits. All counts are LOWER BOUNDS - silent hand-fixes leave no trace.

RANKED:
1. Work reported done that does not actually run - 81 runtime-failure reports, 28 explicitly STILL broken after a fix, 41 browser-verification requests, 15 repos. Dwarfs everything else.
2. NEW - The done report is not trusted: Frank routes finished work to a second adversarial reviewer (be critical / assume mistakes were made) - 66 instances, ~20 repos. Same root cause as #1 from the other side.
3. Skills produce or permit the wrong pattern - 14 instances, 4 repos. Two modes: skill encodes a wrong rule vs. skill was right and the agent diverged. Concentrated in the HFS Angular-migration skill family.
4. NEW - i18n/translation keys missed, invented instead of reused, or left un-wired - 15 instances, 6 HFS worktrees, 9 months.
5. Not reusing existing code / duplicating - 16 instances, 9 repos. This is what the SOLID complaint actually is.
6. Comments that should not have been written - 7 instances in 10 months, 5 repos. Real but ~1 per 6 weeks, and contradicted twice (Frank asked FOR comments in ~/ds/analysis).

REFUTED - SOLID (H2): 4 hits, every one is Frank requesting review AGAINST SOLID up front. ZERO instances of him naming a SOLID principle to correct finished code.

METHOD NOTE for future mining: zero matches for 'you didn't' / 'I said' / 'that is not what I asked' across all 8,007 prompts. Frank never uses blame language - signal lives in 'still ...', 'it doesn't work', 'I see that ...'.

CAVEATS: cass semantic unavailable (consent required) and index mid-rebuild (189/9037) - cass used for spot checks only, never for counts. Transcript adjacency evidence is recency-biased.

title: Baseline the loaded-context token count
description:
## Question

Measure what this setup costs in context before anything changes: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` + `~/CLAUDE.md` + `RTK.md`, each agent file at spawn, and the preloaded skills for `orchestrator`, `worker`, `notes`, `docs`, `ast-search`.

Record per-file and total token counts somewhere durable so the after-measurement is comparable. Decide the counting method (tokenizer vs. a stable proxy) and write it down — an inconsistent method makes the comparison worthless.

Do this early: once tickets start editing files, the "before" is gone.
notes:
RESOLVED. Durable record: docs/context-baseline-2026-08-10.md (in this repo, under docs/agents/).

METHOD (must be reused for the after-measurement): no tokenizer is installed (tiktoken/transformers/ttok/tokencount all absent), so est_tokens = round(chars/4). Raw chars/words/lines recorded per file so a real tokenizer can re-derive later without redoing file selection. Symlinks resolved before reading.

TOTALS: 28 files, 21,957 est tokens.
  always-loaded  4 files   2,189   (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md 792, ~/CLAUDE.md 1,095, RTK.md 240, MEMORY.md 62)
  agent defs    14 files  10,829
  skills        10 files   8,939

HEADLINE FINDING - this reframes the CLAUDE.md ticket. The entire always-loaded set is 2,189 est tokens, about 0.2% of a 1M window. An 80%-reduction rewrite of CLAUDE.md recovers ~1,750 tokens per session, which is close to noise.

Meanwhile per-spawn costs:
  notes         6,896  (def 861 + obsidian-bases 3,220 + obsidian-markdown 1,342 + obsidian-cli 794 + obsidian-markdown-tables 679)
  orchestrator  4,728  (def 2,578 + 4 orchestration skills 2,150)
  worker        1,889   search 1,169   ast-search 1,052   build-runner 726   docs 725
  lsp-search 655  reviewer 551  curl 488  browser 426  codex-review 336  git 309  docker 240

The notes agent costs 3x the entire always-loaded set on every spawn, to write a note. obsidian-bases alone (3,220 tokens, 498 lines) is larger than CLAUDE.md + RTK.md + MEMORY.md combined. notes runs on haiku with 2,637 recorded tool calls.

CONCLUSION: the progressive-disclosure argument from the context-engineering post applies far more to agent frontmatter 'skills:' preloading than to CLAUDE.md. A skill loaded on demand costs nothing until used; a skill in 'skills:' frontmatter is paid on every spawn regardless of whether the task touches it.

GOTCHA for re-measurement: the plugin cache nests THREE levels (cache/<marketplace>/<plugin>/<version>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md), not two. A two-level glob silently misses defuddle and the three obsidian-* skills.

title: Claude 5 setup overhaul
description:
## Destination

A Claude-5-generation rewrite of this setup — `CLAUDE.md`, the 14 custom agents, and the enforcement/verification harness — applied **in place** in `~/.dotfiles`, where every surviving rule names the failure it prevents, the recurring manual corrections are replaced by verification-loop skills, and model/effort routing is explicit.

Done when: the harness enforces what the prose claims, the three recurring corrections are caught by loops instead of by hand, and nothing remains in `CLAUDE.md` or an agent file that cannot name a failure it prevents.

## Notes

**Domain:** personal Claude Code harness (`~/.dotfiles/claude/.claude/`), symlinked into `~/.claude/`.

**Execution is in scope.** This map overrides Wayfinder's plan-don't-do default: tickets may end in applied edits, not just decisions.

**Standing preferences (settled during charting):**

- **Evidence over guidance.** The four Anthropic sources are one input, not the target state. Diverge wherever local evidence contradicts them, and write the divergence down with its justification. Every surviving rule must name a concrete failure it prevents; rules that cannot name one get deleted.
- **Loops over prose rules.** Recurring manual corrections become verification-loop skills that check and fix against a diff — not more instructions.
- **Opus over Fable.** All models and effort levels are available, but Fable has limited capacity. Opus 5 is the default top tier and the advisor tier.
- **Measurement:** loaded-context token count for before/after, plus a session-reflection skill. No formal eval harness.

**Skills every session should consult:** `/grilling`, `/domain-modeling`. Use `/prototype` for the verification-loop tickets.

**Sources this effort is reacting to:**

- [The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models](https://claude.com/blog/the-new-rules-of-context-engineering-for-claude-5-generation-models)
- [Building verification loops in Claude Code with skills](https://claude.com/blog/building-verification-loops-in-claude-code-with-skills)
- [Claude models explained: choosing the best model for your use case](https://claude.com/blog/claude-models-explained-choosing-the-best-model-for-your-use-case)
- [A field guide to Claude Fable: finding your unknowns](https://claude.com/blog/a-field-guide-to-claude-fable-finding-your-unknowns)

**Charting-session findings that motivated this map:**

- The enforcement layer is dead code. `settings.json` wires only `claude-capture`, `rtk hook claude`, `hooked budget`, and `bd prime`. Zero references to `claude-hook-guard`, `enforce-orchestrator.sh`, `enforce-explore-delegation.sh`, or `scope-search.sh` in `settings.json` or `settings.local.json`. `settings.json.bak` references `claude-hook-guard` twice — and `claude/.claude/settings.json` has an uncommitted `-66/+17` diff. 660 lines of `rules.toml`, 19 profiles and ~45 command categories currently enforce nothing.
- Nine agent files defer to a rule engine that is not running: `worker.md:50-51`, `worker.md:99`, `orchestrator.md:38`, `orchestrator.md:193`, `git.md:14`, `docker.md:15`, `browser.md:15`, `reviewer.md:16`, `curl.md:10`.
- 11 of 14 agents are unversioned — only `orchestrator`, `search`, `worker` are symlinked into `~/.dotfiles`.
- Verification discipline is stated four times (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md:38-44`, `orchestrator.md:173-178`, `worker.md:99`, `search.md:75-76`); task sizing twice, near-verbatim (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md:26-34`, `orchestrator.md:64-72`).
- `bd`'s dependency subsystem is broken: `bd dep list`, `bd stats`, all `bd dep --blocks` writes, every parent-child dependency row, **and `bd close` itself** fail with `Error 1105: column "depends_on_id" could not be found in any table in scope`. `bd close` refuses because it cannot check blockers; `bd update --status closed` is the working substitute.

## Blocking — body-convention fallback

`bd`'s dependency subsystem is non-functional for both reads and writes (all 11 `bd dep --blocks` calls failed with `Error 1105`, and every parent-child dependency row failed to write at creation time — the tree still renders, but the dependency rows do not exist). Blocking is therefore recorded as a `BLOCKED BY:` line in each blocked ticket's notes, **not** as native edges, and `bd ready` cannot be trusted as the frontier query.

Once _Repair bd's broken dependency graph_ closes, convert these to native edges and delete this section.

| Ticket | Blocked by |
| --- | --- |
| Decide how much delegation-first survives Claude 5 | Restore the gutted settings.json and rewire the enforcement guard |
| Close the reported-done-but-does-not-run gap | Bring the 11 unversioned agents under version control |
| Design the reuse-before-writing loop | Bring the 11 unversioned agents… |
| Design the model and effort routing policy | Bring the 11 unversioned agents… |
| Design the comment-hygiene verification loop | Bring the 11 unversioned agents… |
| Rewrite CLAUDE.md under evidence-over-guidance | Bring the 11 unversioned agents…; Restore the gutted settings.json…; Decide how much delegation-first survives…; Baseline the loaded-context token count |

**Frontier right now:** _Repair bd's broken dependency graph_, _Bring the 11 unversioned agents under version control_, _Restore the gutted settings.json and rewire the enforcement guard_, _Baseline the loaded-context token count_, _Decide whether adversarial review should be automatic_, _Diagnose why skill-driven output still lands wrong_, _Design the i18n key verification loop_, _Design the session-reflection skill_.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket -->

- **Mine session history for recurring correction patterns** (`dotfiles_nvim-tabs-sidebar-vtq.5`) — Measured 8,007 typed prompts: the dominant failure is **work reported done that does not actually run** (81 reports, 28 still-broken-after-fix, 41 browser requests, 15 repos), and its mirror image, **Frank routing finished work to an adversarial critic** (66 instances, ~20 repos). **SOLID is refuted** — zero post-hoc corrections; what he actually types is "use the shared thing that already exists" (16 instances). **Comments are real but ~1 per 6 weeks** and contradicted twice. Two unnamed patterns surfaced: **i18n keys** (15, 6 worktrees) and reuse. Full asset: `docs/agents/correction-patterns-2026-08-10.md`.

## Not yet specified

- **How `CLAUDE.md` should split.** There are two overlapping files today — `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (51 lines, global) and `~/CLAUDE.md` (103 lines, project) — plus an `@RTK.md` import. Whether this stays two files, collapses to one, or re-splits along a different seam depends on what survives the rewrite.
- **Whether the 14-agent fleet should shrink.** `search`, `ast-search`, and `lsp-search` are three agents distinguished only by tool surface; Claude 5 may pick the right tool itself. Cannot be judged until the delegation-first decision lands.
- **Progressive disclosure for agent prose.** The context-engineering post says to move guidance into skills loaded on demand rather than upfront prompt text. Several agent files are long enough to be candidates, but which parts are hot-path vs. rare is unknown until the rewrite exposes it.
- **Whether the telemetry/provenance system still earns its keep.** `handoff-provenance.md`, `harvest_findings.py`, the coverage JSON contract, and the truncation-recovery protocol in `orchestrator.md:152-171` are substantial machinery built around subagent-report distrust. Its value depends entirely on how much delegation survives.
- **Chaining the verification loops end-to-end.** Once individual loops exist, the verification-loops post's chained pattern applies. Cannot be specified until there are loops to chain.
- **Whether RTK still pays for itself.** A token-reduction proxy has a different value proposition against a 1M context window. Needs the token-count baseline first.
- **Whether the session-reflection skill runs on a schedule or on demand.** Raised during charting; the trigger question is downstream of what the skill actually inspects.

<!-- surfaced 2026-08-10 while working the guard ticket -->

- **Whether the guard should fail open on an invalid config.** `src/main.rs:126-131` fails **closed** — a config that does not validate denies every tool call from every agent, which nearly bricked the setup once already. For advisory infrastructure that is probably wrong, but the answer depends on whether the guard is ever meant to be a security boundary or only a nudge — which is the delegation decision. Not sharp until that lands.
- **Whether `profiles.main` should exist at all.** It is near-dead code: `profiles.orchestrator` has `aliases = ["", "orchestrator"]`, so the real main agent resolves to *orchestrator* and `profiles.main` only fires on a literal `"main"`. Deleting it is tempting, but `engine.rs:92`'s bespoke "Delegate Glob/Grep to the search profile" message is gated on the same `"main"` id and therefore also never fires. The two are entangled and both hang on the delegation policy.
- **Whether `tests/config_policy_tests.rs` is the policy spec of record.** Three of its clauses now conflict with the widened profiles (orchestrator Bash beyond bd, `profiles.main` bd-write, a changed denial message) and a fourth conflicts with the uncommitted `gh-pr` widening for `worker`. Each is a separate decision — amend the test or narrow the policy — and each depends on the delegation policy, so this cannot be phrased as one question yet.
- **What to do with the red agent-registry verification loop.** `tests/agent_registry_tests.rs::agent_registry_is_consistent` cross-checks `CLAUDE.md` against the agent files and is currently failing (stale `Explore` reference; `CLAUDE.md` does not mention `agents/browser.md`). This is already a verification loop of exactly the kind this effort wants more of — but whether to repair it, extend it, or replace it depends on what `CLAUDE.md` becomes.

## Out of scope

- **A formal eval harness for the setup.** More work than the setup itself; token count plus a week of judgment is the agreed bar.
- **Beads workflow redesign** beyond repairing the dependency graph.
- **Obsidian vault conventions and the `notes` agent's CLI contract** — orthogonal to the Claude-5 rewrite.
- **RTK internals.** Whether to keep it is in the fog above; how it works is not this effort's business.

title: Research: does the neovim MCP server support tabpage/window/buffer-scoped queries?
description: For the 'Neovim-aware Claude Code session' design (one nvim instance, tabs as workspaces, one Claude session per tab), the linchpin is whether mcp__neovim__* tools can be scoped to a specific tabpage/window/buffer or whether they are global/active-buffer-only. If active-only, background sessions will read whatever tab the USER is focused on (cross-tab cross-talk), and scoping must fall back to cwd filtering. Identify the server source/package, inspect each tool's schema, and determine scoping capability.
acceptance_criteria: For each mcp__neovim__ tool, classified as (a) global, (b) active-window/buffer, or (c) accepts an explicit tabpage/window/buffer scope param. Source cited file:line. Clear yes/no conclusion: can a query be pinned to a specific tabpage.
notes:
VERIFIED from live MCP tool schemas loaded into this session (authoritative for the connected server version). The scoping primitive is the BUFFER (number or file path); NO tool exposes a tabpage or window parameter.

Per-tool classification:
- nvim_list_buffers: GLOBAL (no params) -> returns ALL buffers across ALL tabs. Entries include file name/path => filterable by cwd prefix.
- nvim_get_cursor_position: ACTIVE-only (no params), 'what are you looking at?' -> follows the user's focused window. UNRELIABLE for a background session in a shared instance. Avoid.
- nvim_get_diagnostics: optional buffer (number|path) + severity; omit = all buffers.
- nvim_get_document_symbols / nvim_lsp_hover / nvim_lsp_definition / nvim_get_lsp_status: optional buffer (number|path); default to CURRENT (active) buffer when omitted.
- nvim_get_buffer_content: REQUIRES buffer (number|path).

CONCLUSION: Cannot pin a query to a tabpage/window. CAN pin to a buffer by file path. => Workspace scoping must use CWD/FILE-PATH filtering: always pass an explicit buffer under the session cwd, filter nvim_list_buffers by cwd prefix, never rely on nvim_get_cursor_position or omitted-buffer defaults (they follow user focus = wrong tab).
close_reason: Research complete; scoping capability determined and recorded in notes.

title: lua_ls: typed signatures from lazydev-injected plugin libraries not resolving
description:
Hovering/go-to-definition on plugin functions accessed via require() (e.g. cli.toggle where local cli = require('sidekick.cli')) produces no typed signature in the nvim config, even though lazydev correctly injects the plugin's lua dir into lua_ls workspace.library. Goal: get typed signatures (sidekick.cli.toggle(opts?: sidekick.cli.Show) + the fun(name:string) overload) to resolve for lazydev-injected plugin requires.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Open ~/.config/nvim/lua/kickstart/plugins/sidekick.lua (which has 'local cli = require("sidekick.cli")').
2. Put cursor on cli.toggle and run :lua vim.lsp.buf.definition() -> 'No locations found'.
3. Hover (K) on cli.toggle -> no typed signature.
Contrast: opening ~/.local/share/nvim/site/pack/core/opt/sidekick.nvim/lua/sidekick/cli/init.lua and hovering M.toggle (~line 100) DOES show the typed signature. So lua_ls reads the annotations but does not resolve the require() into the library.
design:
CONFIRMED working (do not re-investigate):
- nvim uses native vim.pack (NOT lazy.nvim). sidekick.nvim at ~/.local/share/nvim/site/pack/core/opt/sidekick.nvim.
- lazydev attaches ONLY to clients named EXACTLY 'lua_ls' or 'emmylua_ls' (hardcoded, not configurable) -- lazydev/lsp.lua:6, buf.lua:31-50. Client was 'luals' (from lsp/luals.lua filename) so lazydev never attached. FIXED: renamed lsp/luals.lua -> lsp/lua_ls.lua and init.lua:132 'luals' -> 'lua_ls'.
- lazydev now WORKS: ':LazyDev' shows sidekick.nvim/lua and snacks.nvim/lua injected into Lua.workspace.library.
- Added lazydev library entry { path='sidekick.nvim', mods={'sidekick'} } in kickstart/plugins/lazydev.lua (belt-and-suspenders).
- sidekick.cli.Show defined at cli/init.lua:25-29 (fields name?, focus?, filter?, all?); toggle annotated at :98-100.

REMAINING SYMPTOM: lua_ls has the library CONFIGURED but has not SCANNED it into its require map. Direct-open works (parsed on open); cross-module require resolution fails.
acceptance_criteria: In a normal nvim config file, go-to-definition on cli.toggle jumps to sidekick/cli/init.lua and hover shows 'sidekick.cli.toggle(opts?: sidekick.cli.Show)' plus the fun(name:string) overload. Typed signatures resolve generally for lazydev-injected plugin requires.
notes:
NEXT DIAGNOSTIC STEPS (unfinished):
1. Confirm lua_ls finished async library preload before testing (':lua =vim.lsp.status()'). Library list is large. Retry go-to-def once idle.
2. Cross-check require('snacks') go-to-def (snacks.nvim/lua also injected). snacks works but sidekick fails => sidekick-specific. Both fail => general runtime-injected-library scan problem.
3. Restart lua_ls (no :LspRestart in native LSP): :lua vim.lsp.stop_client(vim.lsp.get_clients({name='lua_ls'}), true) then :edit. Let it fully load, then test.
4. Suspect lua_ls 3.15.0 does not re-scan library dirs added mid-session via lazydev didChangeConfiguration poke; clean client start or lua_ls cache clear may be needed.
Highest-ranked hypothesis: async preload timing / runtime-added library not scanned.

title: Design the comment-hygiene verification loop
description:
## Question

The most-repeated manual correction. The context-engineering post uses exactly this rule as its example of over-constraint to delete, and Claude Code's current system prompt already says "write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density" — yet the corrections continue. So a prose rule is not the answer; a loop is.

Prototype a skill that reads the current diff, flags comments that restate the code or narrate the change, and strips them — leaving comments that carry non-obvious why.

Decide: what exactly distinguishes a comment worth keeping, standalone vs. embedded in the producing skills, and whether it runs on the diff or on whole files.
notes:
BLOCKED BY: Bring the 11 unversioned agents under version control (dotfiles_nvim-tabs-sidebar-vtq.2)
DOWNGRADED P1 -> P3 on evidence. The research found only 7 comment-removal requests in 10 months across 5 repos - roughly one per six weeks, against 81 runtime-failure reports. The felt weight far exceeded the measured frequency.

It also found direct counter-evidence: Frank asked FOR comments twice in ~/ds/analysis (R/Shiny) - 'Could you use comments per block to explain the what, why and how?' (history.jsonl:7395) - and once for a ticket-linking marker (:4860). So a blanket no-comments rule would be WRONG.

The evidence-supported rule is narrower than the original ticket assumed: no comments in production Java/TS/spec/SQL code; comments fine in analysis scripts and as ticket-linking markers. That is a context-sensitive rule, which is exactly the kind the context-engineering post says to leave to judgment.

Reconsider whether this needs a loop at all, or just a one-line scoped preference. Frank already tried fixing it at source once: 'The skill should mention that the agent should avoid writing comments unless its absolutely required because of the complexitiy' (history.jsonl:2625).
